claims.claim: Hominins are the fossil species on the human side of the split from the other great apes; humans and the African great apes (chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas) share a common ancestor that lived between 8 and 6 million years ago.

Bipedalism, walking upright on two legs, is the signature trait of the hominin branch: the Smithsonian calls it one of the earliest defining human traits, and SAPIENS calls it a hallmark of human evolution; only humans use upright walking as their primary way of moving.

The oldest evidence for walking on two legs comes from fossils of the earliest known humans: by 6 million years ago upright walking was present, Sahelanthropus may have walked on two legs 7-6 million years ago, and with Australopithecus (about 4 to 2 million years ago) hominins became committed bipeds.
Why bipedalism evolved is debated: scientists still know little about the circumstances that led to the trait's emergence, and the fossil record from the 7-to-4-million-year window is thin.

Sahelanthropus tchadensis lived between 7 and 6 million years ago in West-Central Africa (Chad) and is one of the oldest known species in the human family tree; its skull (known only from cranial material) suggests it may have walked upright, and it may have lived in diverse habitats including forests and grasslands.

Australopithecus afarensis lived between about 3.85 and 2.95 million years ago in eastern Africa, is best known from the 'Lucy' skeleton at Hadar and the oldest documented bipedal footprint trails at Laetoli, and walked upright with a small brain while retaining tree-climbing adaptations.

Paranthropus boisei lived from about 2.3 to 1.2 million years ago in eastern Africa and had a skull specialized for heavy chewing; its type specimen, the 'Zinj' skull, was found by Mary Leakey in 1959 at Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania.

Stone tools appear in the record: by 2.6 million years ago early humans in East Africa struck hammerstones against stone cores to produce sharp flakes, and the oldest known tools, from Lomekwi, Kenya, date to 3.3 million years ago.

Who made the earliest stone tools is debated: the long-standing hypothesis that only the genus Homo made tools is now questioned because the oldest tools predate the oldest known Homo fossils by roughly half a million years, with Australopithecus among the candidates.

Early hominins lived in varied habitats: the earliest upright walkers got around in diverse habitats including forests and grasslands, and East African environments fluctuated widely between moist and dry over the past 6 million years, shaping hominin adaptations.

The hominin fossil record is fragmentary: preservation requires very specific conditions, key time windows have few sites, scientists disagree about how early human species relate to one another, and most early human species left no living descendants.

Human evolution is the lengthy process by which people originated from apelike ancestors, and the traits shared by all people today took about 6 million years to accumulate; early hominins are therefore the deep ancestors of every living human, not failed versions of us.

positions: researchers have proposed several explanations, none settled

conflictingEvidence.issue: Who made the earliest stone tools
positions: long-standing hypothesis: only the genus Homo (e.g., Homo habilis) made stone tools
Lomekwi tools (3.3 mya) and Dikika butchery marks (3.4 mya) predate the oldest Homo fossils by roughly half a million years, so Australopithecus is among the candidates
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states factually that stone tools appear by about 3.3-2.6 million years ago and presents the identity of the earliest toolmakers as genuinely debated.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Sahelanthropus tchadensis is a hominin
positions: Smithsonian species page: one of the oldest known species in the human family tree, possibly walking upright
Smithsonian also flags the open question of whether it is a common ancestor of humans and chimpanzees rather than a hominin proper
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents Sahelanthropus factually as among the oldest known species in the human family tree, with upright walking described as 'may have,' and notes the working nature of the definition.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Human Evolution — The Smithsonian Institution's Human Origins Program
sourceRecords.provider: Smithsonian Institution, National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins Program
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: human evolution as the lengthy process by which people originated from apelike ancestors; bipedalism as one of the earliest defining human traits, evolving over 4 million years ago; humans and African great apes sharing a common ancestor that lived between 8 and 6 million years ago; fossils of early humans between 6 and 2 million years ago coming entirely from Africa; scientists recognizing some 15-20 early human species and disagreeing about relationships; most early human species leaving no living descendants. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Walking Upright — The Smithsonian Institution's Human Origins Program
sourceRecords.provider: Smithsonian Institution, National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins Program
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: the oldest evidence for walking on two legs coming from fossils of the earliest humans known (by about 6 million years ago); Sahelanthropus possibly walking on two legs 7-6 million years ago; early humans combining climbing and walking to get around in diverse habitats and cope with changing climates; Australopithecus walking upright most of the time while still climbing trees. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Sahelanthropus tchadensis — The Smithsonian Institution's Human Origins Program
sourceRecords.provider: Smithsonian Institution, National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins Program
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: Sahelanthropus tchadensis as one of the oldest known species in the human family tree, living between 7 and 6 million years ago in West-Central Africa (Chad); known only from cranial material (nine specimens, found 2001); foramen magnum position indicating upright walking; walking upright possibly helping the species survive in diverse habitats including forests and grasslands; researchers debating whether it is a hominin or a common ancestor of humans and chimpanzees. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Australopithecus afarensis — The Smithsonian Institution's Human Origins Program
sourceRecords.provider: Smithsonian Institution, National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins Program
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: Australopithecus afarensis living between about 3.85 and 2.95 million years ago in Eastern Africa (Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania); best known from Hadar (the 'Lucy' skeleton), Dikika, and Laetoli (oldest documented bipedal footprint trails); walking upright with a small brain (about one-third the size of a modern human brain) and long, strong arms adapted for climbing. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (per subject source-map). Read live 2026-08-22 (SAPIENS archive, article by Briana Pobiner, 23 Feb 2016).
